title: Time delay and the Padé model

sections.figure_alt: A flat magnitude trace and a phase trace that falls as frequency rises.
sections.body_md:
A pure delay holds the signal for \(T_d\) seconds and then releases it unchanged. Nothing about the shape is filtered. In the Laplace domain that hold is a factor \(e^{-s T_d}\). On the frequency axis the magnitude is exactly 1, and the phase is a straight lag proportional to frequency.

The symbol \(T_d\) is the delay. It is not a sample period, and it is not a disturbance. Loops feel the lag at crossover, where a few degrees decide the phase margin. A rational stand-in, the Padé model, is what you use when a design tool wants poles and zeros.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[
e^{-j\omega T_d} = 1 \cdot e^{-j\omega T_d}.
\]
The phase in radians is \(-\omega T_d\). In degrees, multiply by \(180/\pi\). The first-order Padé model is
\[
\frac{1 - s T_d/2}{1 + s T_d/2},
\]
with a pole at \(-2/T_d\) and a zero at \(+2/T_d\). It is an all-pass. The delay margin of a loop is the phase margin, in radians, divided by the crossover frequency.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take \(T_d = 0.12\) seconds and read it at \(3\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). The phase is \(-0.36\) radians, which is about \(-20.63\) degrees. The first-order Padé model of this same delay puts its pole at \(-2/0.12 \approx -16.67\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) and its zero at the mirror image, about \(+16.67\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). Near the origin the rational phase tracks the pure delay. Far above the pole the rational phase levels off, while the pure delay keeps falling.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The product \(\omega T_d\) is in radians. Quoting it as degrees understates the lag by \(180/\pi\). The delay margin has the same trap: divide the margin in radians, not in degrees, by \(\omega_c\). A Padé zero in the right half-plane does not mean the approximation is an unstable system. The pole is in the left half-plane and the magnitude is 1. And a sample period, the \(T\) in \(z = e^{sT}\), shifts a sequence by one tick. It is not this transport delay.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Delay is one of the hard limits on how high a crossover you can ask for. Loop shaping can spend lead to buy some of the phase back, and then the delay spends it again in proportion to the new crossover. The same lag eats the room in a robust-stability test, because a loop that is already close to \(-180^\circ\) has little \(|T|\) left to give a plant disk.
